questions.q: What is the core latency difference between batch and stream ingestion?
options: Batch delivers each individual record faster because it skips per-record scheduling overhead
Stream processes records as they arrive; batch waits to process accumulated data
Batch and stream have equal latency once pipelines are warmed up
Stream latency grows with data volume while batch latency stays constant
questions.explanation: Batch latency is bounded by its collection window plus job runtime, while streaming handles each record on arrival, giving sub-second freshness at higher per-event overhead.

questions.q: Which workload is the classic fit for batch processing?
options: Fraud checks that must block a transaction within milliseconds
Live dashboards updating as user events arrive
Alerting on error spikes within seconds of occurrence
Nightly aggregation of a full day's records into reports
questions.explanation: Nightly reports have no freshness requirement and need complete, settled input, which is exactly what a scheduled batch pass over stored data provides most cheaply.

questions.q: In stream processing, what problem do watermarks address?
options: Deciding when a window can close despite late or out-of-order events
Preventing a fast producer from overwhelming a slower downstream consumer
Encrypting records so downstream consumers can verify integrity
Assigning each event to a partition based on its key
questions.explanation: A watermark is the system's estimate of event-time progress: it declares that events older than a threshold are unlikely to arrive, letting windows emit results.

questions.q: What does 'event time' mean, as opposed to 'processing time'?
options: The moment the stream processor's window fires for the event
The wall-clock time when the record is written to the sink
The time the event actually occurred at its source
The timestamp the message broker assigns on enqueue
questions.explanation: Event time is stamped at the source when the thing happened, so results stay correct and reproducible regardless of network delay or when the pipeline processes it.

questions.q: Why is throughput per unit of compute typically higher in batch than in streaming?
options: Large sequential reads and amortized setup beat per-event overhead
Batch jobs run on faster hardware tiers reserved by schedulers
Streams must encrypt each event, which dominates their CPU cost
Batch frameworks can skip serialization because data already sits at rest
questions.explanation: Batch amortizes planning, I/O, and coordination over millions of rows and reads them sequentially, whereas streaming pays scheduling and bookkeeping cost per record.

questions.q: What is backpressure in a streaming pipeline?
options: Reprocessing old events after a consumer crash wipes its state
The broker compacting a topic to reclaim disk space
A signal to slow producers when consumers can't keep up
Duplicate events created when a producer retries a send
questions.explanation: Backpressure propagates slowness upstream so buffers stay bounded, trading throughput for stability instead of letting queues grow until the system runs out of memory.

questions.q: What does 'at-least-once' delivery imply for consumers?
options: Some events may be silently dropped whenever the broker fails over
Duplicates are possible, so processing should be idempotent
Each event arrives exactly once but possibly out of order
Events arrive in strict order but may be batched together
questions.explanation: At-least-once guarantees no loss by retrying, which necessarily admits redelivery. Consumers must make effects idempotent so a repeat produces the same final state.

questions.q: Which component typically decouples event producers from stream consumers?
options: A distributed lock service coordinating writer leases
A shared relational table polled by every consumer
An API gateway that routes events to consumer replicas
A partitioned, replicated log such as Kafka
questions.explanation: A durable partitioned log buffers events independently of consumers, letting producers write at their own rate and multiple consumers read, replay, and scale separately.

questions.q: A team needs hourly business reports and sub-second anomaly alerts from the same events. What's a sound architecture?
options: One micro-batch job every hour tuned to also emit the alerts
Pure streaming for both, materializing full reports per event
Pure batch for both, shrinking the interval to one minute
A stream path for alerts plus a batch or warehouse path for reports
questions.explanation: The two needs have opposite requirements: alerts want low latency, reports want completeness. Splitting the paths lets each optimize for its own constraint from shared input.

questions.q: Your dashboard counts drop briefly, then correct themselves minutes later. Events are arriving late. Which mechanism produces this correction behavior?
options: Watermarks silently discarding every late event as each window closes
Allowed-lateness updates that re-emit revised window results
Broker retention deleting and restoring recent segments
Consumer rebalancing replaying the entire partition
questions.explanation: Allowed lateness keeps window state alive past the watermark, so late arrivals trigger an updated emission that revises the earlier, incomplete result.

questions.q: A consumer crashes after writing results but before committing its offset. On restart, what happens under at-least-once semantics?
options: The broker detects the partial write and rolls the output back
The event is skipped because the broker saw the delivery attempt
The event is reprocessed, so the write may happen twice
The consumer halts until an operator resolves the conflict
questions.explanation: The committed offset is the only durable record of progress, so the consumer resumes from the older offset and redoes work whose side effects already landed.

questions.q: Which technique gives effectively-exactly-once results on top of at-least-once delivery?
options: Idempotent writes keyed by a stable event ID at the sink
Doubling consumer replicas so another instance verifies each write
Switching the broker over to fire-and-forget publishing
Compressing events so duplicates collapse into one message
questions.explanation: Deduplicating at the sink with a stable key makes repeated delivery harmless, achieving exactly-once effects without needing exactly-once transport.

questions.q: Reprocessing 90 days of history after a logic bug is trivial in one paradigm and painful in the other. Which statement captures it?
options: Streams replay faster because their events are already ordered
Batch reprocessing requires replaying the broker log at original speed
Batch re-runs over stored input easily; streams need replayable retention and state rebuilds
Neither can reprocess without vendor-specific snapshot tooling
questions.explanation: Batch inputs sit immutably in storage, so you just re-run the job. Streaming backfill needs the log to still retain 90 days plus a way to rebuild operator state.

questions.q: Event counts differ between your streaming output and a batch recount of the same day. Which is the usual authoritative choice, and why?
options: Batch, because it reads the complete, settled input after late data lands
Streaming, because its watermarks certify that no late events were ever missed
Streaming, because broker offsets provide exactly-once accounting
Batch, because batch frameworks checksum every record they read
questions.explanation: Batch runs after the fact over the full dataset, so it sees late arrivals the streaming windows already closed on. Watermarks are heuristics and cannot certify completeness.

questions.q: Micro-batching (small periodic batches) primarily trades what for what?
options: Durability for throughput, buffering events in volatile memory
Some latency for higher throughput and simpler delivery accounting
Ordering guarantees for lower end-to-end processing cost
Schema flexibility for compatibility with columnar storage formats
questions.explanation: Grouping events into small batches amortizes per-record overhead and lets offsets commit per batch, buying efficiency and simpler recovery at the cost of added delay.

questions.q: A streaming job keyed by user_id holds 30 days of per-user state. What is the main operational cost this introduces?
options: The message broker must retain thirty days of every topic in the cluster
Consumers can no longer scale beyond one instance per topic
Each event must be re-sorted by key before processing
Large state must be checkpointed and restored on failure or rescale
questions.explanation: Long-lived keyed state turns the job stateful: checkpoints grow large, recovery means reloading them, and rescaling requires redistributing state across new partitions.

questions.q: A window closes at watermark, but 0.5% of events arrive after it. The business demands complete daily numbers. Which design is standard?
options: Emit streaming results as provisional and reconcile with a later batch pass
Set the watermark delay to 24 hours so windows capture everything
Reject late events at ingestion so totals never change after close
Store late events in a dead-letter queue reviewed manually each week
questions.explanation: Serving fast provisional numbers and correcting them with an authoritative batch recount satisfies both freshness and completeness; a 24-hour watermark destroys the latency benefit.

questions.q: Exactly-once 'end to end' still breaks when your sink is an external email API. Why?
options: Email payloads exceed the maximum transactional message size
Brokers cannot retain events long enough for email retries
The send is a non-transactional side effect that can't roll back or dedupe
Watermarks cannot be computed for events leaving the cluster
questions.explanation: Exactly-once relies on committing output atomically with progress. A sent email cannot be unsent or joined to the checkpoint, so a retry after a crash sends it twice.

questions.q: Throughput is fine on average, but one partition lags badly. Keying is by customer_id and one customer dominates traffic. Best fix?
options: Increase partition count so the big customer's data spreads out automatically
Raise consumer memory so the hot partition buffers more events
Switch to round-robin keying and drop per-customer ordering everywhere
Salt the hot key into sub-keys, then re-aggregate downstream
questions.explanation: One key always hashes to one partition, so adding partitions cannot split it. Salting fans the hot customer across several sub-keys, with a second stage merging the partials.

questions.q: You can deliver a feature with a 6-hour batch job or a streaming pipeline costing 4x more to run and operate. What should drive the decision?
options: Streaming is the modern default choice, so choosing batch should require justification
Whether fresher-than-6-hours data changes a real decision or outcome
Whichever option the team's existing scheduler supports natively
Batch always wins on cost, so streaming needs executive approval
questions.explanation: Freshness is only worth its cost if someone acts on the newer data. Tie the latency requirement to a concrete decision, then pick the cheapest design that meets it.
